overview.title: Concept drift, learning from the past, and sampling bias
overview.chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning
overview.main_topic: Two forms of nonrepresentative data: concept drift over time, and sampling bias from the collection process
overview.central_idea: Training data can stop being representative over time (concept drift), and it can be unrepresentative from the start because the way you collect it is correlated with what you predict (sampling bias). In both cases the model only recognizes patterns it has seen and assumes the future resembles the past.
overview.importance: These are two of the most common ways a model that tested well fails in production. Concept drift sets the model's shelf life (p.212), and sampling bias can quietly invalidate an entire dataset.
learning_objectives: Define concept drift and give the book's examples (2013 music recommender, 2011 IMDB data, credit card fraud).
Explain why adversarial settings make drift especially fast, and what fast drift requires.
Explain the assumption behind predicting the future from past data.
Define sampling bias as a collection process that interacts with the target.
Retell the 1948 'Dewey Defeats Truman' phone-survey example and why the phone sample was biased.
prerequisites: Representative data and the dish-photo example (p.200).
The IMDB dataset (chapter 4) and the example projects (p.195-196).

summary:
The page finishes the discussion of **nonrepresentative data** from p.200 with two more cases.

**Concept drift** happens when "the properties of the production data change over time, causing model accuracy to gradually decay." It is especially common with user-generated data. The book's examples:

- a **music recommender trained in 2013** "may not be very effective today";
- the **IMDB dataset was collected in 2011**, so a model trained on it would probably do worse on 2020 reviews than on 2012 reviews, "as vocabulary, expressions, and movie genres evolve over time";
- drift is **particularly acute in adversarial contexts** such as **credit card fraud detection**, where "fraud patterns change practically every day."

Fast drift calls for **constant data collection, annotation, and model retraining**.

The authors then state a general limit: ML can only **memorize patterns present in the training data**, and "you can only recognize what you've seen before." Training on the past to predict the future assumes **the future will behave like the past**, which "often isn't the case."

The sidebar **The problem of sampling bias** calls it "a particularly insidious and common case of nonrepresentative data." It occurs when **the data collection process interacts with what you are trying to predict**, which biases the measurements. The historical example is the **1948 US presidential election**. On election night the *Chicago Tribune* printed **"DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN"** based on a **phone survey**, and Truman won. Phone users in 1948 were not a random, representative sample of voters. They were more likely to be richer, conservative and Dewey (Republican) voters. Phone surveys now account for sampling bias. The bias still exists in polling, but pollsters are aware of it and correct for it. The page shows the famous photo of Truman holding up the mistaken headline.

paragraphs.excerpt: user-generated data. Concept drift occurs when the properties of the production data change
paragraphs.what_it_says: Concept drift is when production data properties change over time and model accuracy gradually decays. Examples: a 2013 music recommender may be ineffective today, and a model trained on the 2011 IMDB data would do worse on 2020 reviews than on 2012 reviews as vocabulary, expressions and genres evolve. Drift is acute in adversarial settings like credit card fraud, where patterns change nearly every day. Fast drift requires constant data collection, annotation and retraining.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A dataset is a snapshot of a world that keeps changing. The model's mapping is frozen at training time, so the gap between the snapshot and reality grows. In adversarial domains the opponent changes behavior specifically to avoid detection, which makes drift fast and deliberate.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It turns ML from a one-off build into an ongoing process. Model maintenance (p.212) and continued annotation (p.213) follow directly from it.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the literature separates covariate shift (p(x) changes), label or prior shift (p(y) changes) and concept drift in the narrow sense (p(y|x) changes). The book uses 'concept drift' broadly for any change in production data properties over time.

terminology.meaning: Change over time in the properties of production data that causes model accuracy to gradually decay.
A setting where an opponent (e.g., fraudsters) actively adapts to evade the model.
Fitting the model again on fresh data so it reflects current patterns.

connections: p.200: concept drift introduced as a phenomenon related to nonrepresentative data.
p.212: model lifespans: weeks for the music recommender, days for fraud detection, a couple of years at best for image search.

paragraphs.excerpt: Keep in mind that machine learning can only be used to memorize patterns
paragraphs.what_it_says: ML can only memorize patterns present in its training data, so you can only recognize what you've seen before. Predicting the future from past data assumes the future will behave like the past, which often isn't true.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This sums up both p.200 and the drift discussion. A model contains no knowledge beyond its data, and forecasting is only valid when the world is stationary enough.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets realistic expectations, for example about forecasting markets, where the book later (p.403) says past performance is not a good predictor of future returns.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: this is the stationarity assumption, the implicit premise behind any model trained on historical data and used in the future.

terminology.meaning: The book's phrase for what a model extracts from data; it cannot invent patterns it has not seen.

connections: p.198: stock movements can't be predicted from price history.
p.403: markets vs. weather; 'looking in the rear-view mirror is a bad way to drive.'

paragraphs.excerpt: A particularly insidious and common case of nonrepresentative data is sampling bias.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Sampling bias is an insidious, common case of nonrepresentative data: the collection process interacts with what you are predicting, so the measurements are biased. In 1948 the Chicago Tribune printed 'DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN' from a phone survey, and Truman won. Phone owners then were richer, more conservative and more likely to vote for Dewey. Today every phone survey accounts for sampling bias. It has not disappeared from polling, but pollsters know about it and correct for it.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The key point is that selection is correlated with the target. Owning a phone in 1948 correlated with wealth, and wealth correlated with voting Republican, so sampling by phone over-sampled Dewey voters. No amount of data from that channel fixes the bias. A larger biased sample only makes you more confident in the wrong answer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is 'insidious' because it is invisible inside the dataset. Everything looks consistent until reality disagrees, and a held-out test set drawn the same way will not catch it.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: pollsters correct sampling bias by reweighting responses (post-stratification) so the sample's demographics match the population. The same idea underlies importance weighting under distribution shift in ML.

terminology.meaning: Bias that arises when the data-collection process is correlated with the quantity being predicted.
A sample whose selection is independent of the variable of interest, so it mirrors the population.

connections: p.200: nonrepresentative data as the cardinal sin of data collection.

concepts.name: Concept drift
concepts.definition: Change in the properties of production data over time that causes a trained model's accuracy to gradually decay.
concepts.intuition: The world changes and the model does not, so they slowly drift apart.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: may involve shifts in p(x), p(y) or p(y|x). Mitigated by monitoring, continuous data collection and annotation, and periodic retraining.
concepts.significance: Present in almost all real-world problems; it determines how long a model stays useful.
concepts.example: A 2013 music recommender today; 2011 IMDB model on 2020 reviews; daily-changing fraud patterns.
concepts.misconception: A model that was accurate at launch stays accurate.

concepts.name: Sampling bias
concepts.definition: A form of nonrepresentative data in which the data-collection process interacts with what you are trying to predict, producing biased measurements.
concepts.intuition: If the way you choose who to ask is linked to their answer, you get a skewed answer.
concepts.technical: Selection is correlated with the target; the observed distribution differs systematically from the population's.
concepts.significance: Insidious because the data look internally consistent; held-out tests drawn the same way won't reveal it.
concepts.example: 1948 phone survey predicting Dewey; phone owners were richer and more conservative.
concepts.misconception: More data from the same channel fixes the bias; it doesn't.

concepts.name: Representative training data
concepts.definition: Training data that resembles production data; concept drift and sampling bias are two ways it fails.
concepts.intuition: You can only recognize what you've seen before.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: the i.i.d./stationarity assumption linking training and deployment distributions.
concepts.significance: The foundation of data collection work (p.200).
concepts.example: Training on past data to predict the future assumes the future behaves like the past.
concepts.misconception: Past data automatically describes the future.

deeper.title: Why the phone survey went wrong, step by step
deeper.body:
1. **Target**: the vote (Dewey vs. Truman).
2. **Collection channel**: telephone.
3. **Hidden link**: in 1948, owning a phone correlated with being richer and more conservative (book), and those traits correlated with voting Dewey (book).
4. **Result**: the sample over-represents Dewey voters, so the estimate is biased toward Dewey.
5. **Why 'insidious'**: nothing inside the survey data shows the problem. Only comparison with the true population (the election) reveals it.

ML parallel (inference): if you collect app-review data only from users who opt in to feedback, and opting in correlates with being very happy or very angry, a sentiment model will learn a distorted picture of typical users.

deeper.title: Concept drift speed across the chapter's projects
deeper.body: Putting this page together with p.212: the book estimates the music recommender's lifespan at **weeks**, fraud detection at **days** (adversarial drift, as described here), and the image search engine at **a couple of years in the best case**. Inference: the faster the drift, the more the project budget has to go to the continuous collect, annotate, retrain loop the page describes, rather than to the first model.

deeper.title: The rear-view mirror
deeper.body: A model trained on the past is like driving by looking only in the rear-view mirror. On a straight, unchanging road (stationary data) that works surprisingly well. When the road bends (drift) or the mirror shows only part of the road (sampling bias), you crash. The book uses the same image for markets on p.403.

misconceptions.claim: Once a model is deployed with good accuracy, the job is done.
misconceptions.correction: Concept drift gradually degrades accuracy; fast drift requires constant data collection, annotation and retraining.

misconceptions.claim: A large survey or dataset can't be badly biased.
misconceptions.correction: Sampling bias comes from how data are collected, not from how much; the 1948 phone survey was systematically skewed toward Dewey voters.

misconceptions.claim: Machine learning can discover genuinely new patterns that will hold in the future.
misconceptions.correction: The book says ML can only memorize patterns present in its training data; using it for the future assumes the future behaves like the past, which often isn't so.

misconceptions.claim: Sampling bias is a solved historical problem.
misconceptions.correction: The book says it is far from a thing of the past in polling; the difference is that pollsters are now aware of it and correct for it.

earlier.note: Representative data, the dish-photo example, and the first mention of concept drift.
Stock prediction from price history: another case where the past doesn't predict the future.
The credit card fraud and music recommendation projects.

Maintaining your model: lifespans set by concept drift.
Keep collecting and annotating data after launch, focusing on hard samples.
Markets and machine learning: past performance is not a good predictor of future returns.
The IMDb dataset processed from raw text.

takeaways: Concept drift: production data properties change over time and accuracy gradually decays; it shows up in almost all real-world problems.
Drift is fastest in adversarial settings like fraud detection and demands constant collection, annotation and retraining.
ML only memorizes patterns present in training data; predicting the future assumes it behaves like the past.
Sampling bias occurs when the data collection process interacts with the target, as in the 1948 phone survey that predicted Dewey.
Sampling bias is insidious: the data look fine internally, and only awareness and active correction protect you.

questions.question: How does the book define concept drift?
questions.answer: Concept drift occurs when the properties of the production data change over time, causing model accuracy to gradually decay.
questions.explanation: This is the definition at the top of the page, which completes the sentence begun on p.200.

questions.question: In which of the book's examples is concept drift described as 'particularly acute'?
questions.explanation: Fraud is an adversarial context where patterns change practically every day. Music and IMDB are drift examples but not described as acute, and satellite imagery is not discussed here.

questions.question: Why would a model trained on the 2011 IMDB dataset do worse on 2020 reviews than on 2012 reviews?
questions.answer: Because vocabulary, expressions and movie genres evolve over time, so 2020 reviews differ more from the 2011 training data than 2012 reviews do.
questions.explanation: This is the book's explanation. The further production data is in time from the training snapshot, the more it has drifted.

questions.question: What exactly made the 1948 Chicago Tribune phone survey an example of sampling bias?
options: The survey asked too few people
Phone users were more likely to be richer, conservative and Dewey voters, so the collection method was linked to the vote
The survey was conducted too early
questions.answer: Phone users were more likely to be richer, conservative and Dewey voters, so the collection method was linked to the vote
questions.explanation: Sampling bias is defined as the collection process interacting with the target. Sample size, lying and timing are not what the book identifies.

questions.question: What assumption does the book say you make whenever you use ML trained on past data to predict the future, and why is it risky?
questions.answer: That the future will behave like the past. It is risky because this often isn't the case, and ML can only recognize patterns it has seen.
questions.explanation: This is from the 'Keep in mind…' paragraph and connects to concept drift and to the market-forecasting warning on p.403.

questions.question: According to the book, what does dealing with fast concept drift require?
questions.answer: Constant data collection, annotation, and model retraining.
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of the first paragraph.

questions.question: Think of a dataset you know. How was it collected, and could the collection process be correlated with the target? How fast would you expect its domain to drift?
questions.answer: Answers vary; look for selection mechanisms linked to the label (opt-in, specific channels or devices) and for domains with fast-changing behavior.
questions.explanation: This applies both sampling bias and concept drift as checks on your own data.
